title: Xiaomi's Three Chips: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on an On-Device AI Paradigm Shift
dek: Xiaomi has released three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture. It's trading resources for time, betting on an on-device AI paradigm shift and vertical integration, but it still lags top-tier chip companies.
why: This episode offers an in-depth analysis of the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It's dense with information, with clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors following Xiaomi.
who: Investors focused on Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals wanting to understand the on-device AI trend.
skip: The first 3 minutes discussing the definition of self-developed chips can be skipped; go straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Chip capability is about system definition, not IP self-reliance
points.body: To judge whether a company can make chips, don't just count how many IP blocks it hand-crafts; look at how much system definition power it holds. Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, but system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm excel at annual iteration and continuous tape-outs, which latecomers lack. Xiaomi doesn't have a decade to learn slowly, so it chooses an aggressive path, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: O1's poor energy efficiency stems from a missing shared water tank
points.body: The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to spike under heavy GPU load and hurting energy efficiency. An SLC is like a shared water tank in a neighborhood: the closer data is to compute units, the faster access and lower power. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores idle waiting for data—this is the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, split into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, plus an on-chip network scheduler to handle data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's generic bus forces Xuanjie to build its own
points.body: ARM's off-the-shelf CHI+CMN solution is too generic, retaining compatibility and redundancy that hinder customization for Xuanjie. The O3 instead uses a self-developed X-Ring unified fabric, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, with custom high-speed routing hubs and memory controllers. This reduces protocol conversion overhead and lets data decide cache placement and paths based on needs. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead drops 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds, 32% lower than the O1 and even below Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: Compute bottleneck shifts from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP—so computation happens where data resides, reducing data movement. NPU cores drop from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200 Tops, because Xiaomi judges that large-model bottlenecks are expanding from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. Vector units are nearly as large as Tensor units, with 6.8 times the multiply-accumulate units of the O1, and introduce an SMT-like architecture similar to CUDA to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be co-defined by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no accuracy loss, cutting memory bandwidth and capacity needs by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model runs on the O3, with prefill performance up 40% and decode up 45%. This chip-model co-definition capability is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no waiting for others to define models before adapting.

points.h: 3nm performance is squeezed out standard cell by standard cell
points.body: The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% better performance at same power and 5%-10% lower power at same frequency. Xiaomi also made extensive process optimizations: self-developed standard cells grew from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip blocks; compressed power-supply buffer channels so power and signals route through module centers, boosting transistor density by 5%. The CPU changed from 4 clusters to 3 clusters with 10 big cores, improving single-core performance by 31% and multi-core by 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, connected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical interconnects for high bandwidth and lower energy per bit shift, akin to HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, bandwidth 1.22TB/s, far exceeding the tens of bits wide connection of traditional SoC-LPDDR. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: CXMT's value lies not in speed grade but in co-definition
points.body: Xiaomi partners with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing reliance on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT offers the 10.667Gbps entry speed grade, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps with wider channels, larger SLC, and custom memory controllers. More importantly, they co-validate and tune from the design stage, jointly defining China's mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and PHY capabilities, earning a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: Xiaomi is betting not on chips but on a time window
points.body: First, it bets on an on-device computing paradigm shift: AI's weight in SoCs grows, phones become AI interaction gateways, and Xiaomi wants to be a definer. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes a core competency for device companies—generic chips can't meet fragmented needs across people, cars, and homes, so it must own its compute architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window, trading resources for time to compress the catch-up cycle, preferring to bear engineering risk rather than watch the window close.

points.h: Xuanjie closes faster, but still fails all three thresholds
points.body: Top-tier SoC companies need three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitectures, self-developed 5G basebands, and continuous multi-generation tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently meets none, still clearly behind the first tier—it's just closing faster. What truly reshapes the industry isn't a single dazzling chip but the sustained iteration capability built by a group of companies. Xuanjie's larger significance is proving Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stopped and are moving forward with Chinese chip industry partners.

Placing memory close to compute units to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
When data movement capability becomes the performance bottleneck, rendering additional compute cores ineffective.
